newsitem.title: MEXICO: Head of Santander-Mexicano pension firm quits.
newsitem.headline: Head of Santander-Mexicano pension firm quits.

text.p: Santander Investment on Monday said Manuel Reynaud, head of its private pension fund management firm Afore Santander-Mexicano, had quit.
Reynaud was also the first head of the Mexican Pension Fund Association, and his departure was a blow for the fledling private pensions industry, analysts said.
Sources at the Afore, who asked not to be identified, were shocked by the news, saying that the firm had appeared to get off to a strong start in a highly competitive industry.

"Manuel Reynaud presented his resignation and in a very brief period of time we will indicate who it is who will be his replacement," said Jaime de Pinies, spokesman for Santander Investment in Madrid.
De Pinies sought to play down a report in El Financiero newspaper that Reynaud quit because he had to report to two bosses at Santander, in what columnist Herminio Rebollo dubbed the "ham sandwich."
Reynaud was previously part of Grupo Financiero Invermexico. He was named head of the Afore after the Mexican banking grupo was bought by Banco Santander last October.
"I wouldn't put too much stock in that," De Pinies said. "We have not heard that these are the reasons behind his resignation."
Rebollo said the news was bound to shake up Mexico's Afore business, which only started this year and has faced strong criticism for the commissions charged.

"In fact, (Reynaud) has become the first victim of the Afore market, with the added problem that he had been unanimously elected as president of the (industry association) which he will definitely leave," the columnist said.
As president of the association, Reynaud had given a string of interviews in which he was forced to defend the level of commissions. Critics said they were unfairly high.
He had also criticized 96-year-old Mexican labor leader Fidel Velazquez for attacking the private pension funds.

Sources at Afore Santander-Mexicano, that in February launched one of the highest profile publicity blitzes of all Afores, sending out armies of red-uniformed sales staff, said affiliations were going well. They doubted poor performance was behind Reynaud's departure.
Reynaud was not immediately available to comment.
